# Numbers 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Setting

Numbers 15–19 covers the 38 years of wilderness wandering. With a first-generation population of perhaps 600,000+ adult males, an average of roughly 100 deaths per day occurred over those decades — meaning constant contact with dead bodies and therefore constant ceremonial defilement. God mercifully provides an accessible means of purification through the ashes of a red heifer. The chapter falls into two main parts: the ritual of the red heifer (vv. 1–10) and the laws of purification from corpse-uncleanness (vv. 11–22).

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

---

## vv. 1–2 — The Statute of the Red Heifer

**v. 1 — "Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron…"**
In Numbers 18 the LORD spoke to Aaron alone; here He addresses both brothers together, for the matter concerns the whole congregation.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

**v. 2 — "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded…"**

- **Phrasing:** The combination of "statute" (*chuqqah*) and "law" (*torah*) is rare, occurring only here and in Numbers 31:21, underscoring the importance of what follows (Ellicott). The Hebrew *chuqqah* comes from a root meaning "to engrave," suggesting a permanently inscribed decree.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

- **Timing:** Some Jewish commentators (Ibn Ezra) thought this law was originally given before the departure from Sinai; the wording "which the LORD hath commanded" is consistent with a previously existing ordinance (Ellicott). Dummelow notes the immediate trigger may have been the mass deaths from Korah's rebellion (Num 16:49); Josephus connects it with the death of Miriam (Num 20:1).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/numbers-19.html

**"…an unblemished red heifer that has no defect and has never been placed under a yoke."**

- **Female animal:** This is unique among OT sacrifices — normally a male was required. A heifer (*parah*) is a young cow that has never calved. Keil & Delitzsch explain: the female is "the bearer of life" (Gen 3:20), chosen because this sacrifice is an antidote to death, not an atonement for sin *per se*. Constable agrees: "the female was the bearer of life, and continued life is what this sacrifice provided."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/numbers/19.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html

- **Red colour:** The only sacrifice in which colour mattered. Wenham suggests the red colour "resembled blood." Keil & Delitzsch argue the red colour represents "the most intensive life, which has its seat in the blood." Ellicott notes the Hebrew may mean "entirely red" or simply "without spot" (freedom from defect). Clarke observes that in Egyptian religion, red bulls were sacrificed to the evil demon Typhon, so this may have been a deliberate contrast to pagan practice.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

- **No yoke:** The animal must never have been used for common labour — its vital energy uncrippled. Guzik sees a picture of Christ, who was never under the yoke of sin.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

- **Seven red heifers in history:** The Jewish Mishnah says only seven red heifers were offered from Moses to the destruction of the Second Temple (AD 70). The Temple Institute in modern Israel seeks a tenth, believing it necessary for purifying a rebuilt third temple.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

---

## vv. 3–6 — The Slaughter and Burning

**v. 3 — "Give it to Eleazar the priest, and he will have it brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence."**

- **Eleazar, not Aaron:** The high priest could not perform this rite because he was forbidden to incur corpse-related uncleanness (Lev 21:11-12). Eleazar, as Aaron's eldest son and successor, superintends it (Ellicott). The actual slaughter was performed not by the priest but by a layman, with Eleazar witnessing — "before his face" (Keil & Delitzsch).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/numbers/19.htm

- **Outside the camp:** Unlike altar sacrifices, this was done outside the camp — it was more a "slaughtering" than a formal sacrifice (Guzik). Constable notes this was because of the heifer's connection with sin and death. This prefigures Christ suffering "outside the gate" (Heb 13:12).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html

**v. 4 — "Eleazar the priest is to take some of its blood on his finger and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting."**

- This sprinkling is what makes the slaughter a genuine sacrifice, bringing it into relation with the sanctuary (Keil). Seven times indicates completeness. The blood was sprinkled *toward* the Tabernacle, not on the altar — because the entire ceremony took place outside the camp (Ellicott).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/numbers/19.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html

**v. 5 — "Then the heifer must be burned in his sight. Its hide, its flesh, and its blood are to be burned, along with its dung."**

- The whole animal was burned — hide, flesh, blood, and dung together. This is entirely unlike normal sacrifices, where blood was drained at the altar and the animal was cut into pieces. Here the blood remains with the carcass and is burned *with* it, so the ashes would contain blood residue (Guzik). The animal was "wholly consumed" without being flayed, cleaned, or divided (Pulpit Homiletics), suggesting total dedication.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/19.htm

**v. 6 — "The priest is to take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool and throw them onto the burning heifer."**

- These same three items appear in the cleansing ceremony for a leper (Lev 14:4-6). Each carries symbolic weight:
  - **Cedar wood** — resistant to decay and rot; emblem of fragrance and incorruption (Ellicott); possibly prefiguring the wood of the cross (Guzik).
  - **Hyssop** — emblem of purification; used to apply blood at Passover; David's cry "purge me with hyssop" (Ps 51:7) alludes to this rite (Ellicott, Guzik).
  - **Scarlet wool** — colour of blood and life; also emblematic of sin ("though your sins be as scarlet," Isa 1:18) and of the blood that remits sin (Ellicott). Spurgeon notes that according to Maimonides, the cedar was wrapped with hyssop and then enveloped in scarlet, so that what was visible was the scarlet — "the emblem of sin and its punishment."
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

---

## vv. 7–10 — The Paradox of Purification: the Clean Become Unclean

**v. 7 — "Then the priest must wash his clothes and bathe his body in water; after that he may enter the camp, but he will be ceremonially unclean until evening."**

- **The great paradox:** The very rite that produces cleansing for others renders those who perform it unclean. Eleazar, though he only supervised and sprinkled the blood, becomes unclean until evening. This is one of the most striking features of the red heifer ceremony. The Pulpit Commentary says: "Thus God seeks by type and symbol…to impress on us the truth that sin is 'exceeding sinful.' And we are reminded that even our sinless Priest and Sacrifice needed to be 'made sin' for us in order that we might be cleansed."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/19.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

- Ellicott notes the Targum of Jonathan applies this to the priest who killed the heifer; Ibn Ezra to the priest who burned it — but the reference is "more probably to Eleazar."
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html

**v. 8 — "The one who burned the heifer must also wash his clothes…unclean until evening."**

- At least one assistant did the actual burning (since Eleazar merely superintended). He too contracts uncleanness. Precept Austin observes this text "indicates that Eleazar had at least one assistant to do the burning."
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

**v. 9 — "Then a man who is ceremonially clean is to gather up the ashes…store them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp…for preparing the water of purification; this is for purification from sin."**

- **"Water of purification"** — literally "water of separation" (Heb. *mei niddah*), also translated "water for impurity." It separates the unclean person from their uncleanness (Gill). The ashes, normally defiling, are here the instrument of cleansing — "God, who is sovereign, has the authority to abrogate what is normal" (Constable).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html
  - https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/19.htm

- **"Purification from sin"** — the Hebrew calls this a *chattat*, a sin-offering. The ashes carried the virtue of a sin offering without requiring a new animal each time. Guzik calls it "a God-approved shortcut" — building on existing principles of sacrifice but making cleansing instantly accessible.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

**v. 10 — "The man who has gathered up the ashes…must also wash his clothes…unclean until evening. This is a permanent statute for the Israelites and for the foreigner residing among them."**

- Even the man gathering the ashes (already a clean person) becomes unclean until evening. The "permanent statute" extends to the *ger* (sojourner/foreigner). Ellicott sees a foreshadowing: "So the promise of the remission of sins through Christ Jesus was not only to the Jews and to their children, but also to all that were afar off (Acts 2:39)."
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html

---

## vv. 11–13 — Corpse Defilement and the Seven-Day Period

**v. 11 — "Whoever touches any dead body will be unclean for seven days."**

- **Death as supreme defilement:** Contact with a dead *animal* rendered one unclean only until evening (Lev 11:24, 27, 39); a dead *human* body caused seven days' uncleanness. Clarke exclaims: "How low does this lay man!…seven times worse than the vilest animal!" The reason is that human death is the direct wages of sin (Rom 5:12; Gen 2:15-17).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

- Precept Austin sets this in context: with ~1.2 million deaths over 38 years, the Israelites were constantly encountering corpses. Without this provision, the camp would have been perpetually defiled.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

**v. 12 — "He must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day; then he will be clean."**

- The third-day and seventh-day pattern appears elsewhere in Scripture — notably, Jesus rose on the third day. The seventh day (Sabbath) represents completion. The person was not automatically cleansed by time; active purification was required: "The seventh day was not magical, nor did God deem someone clean simply because the time had passed. Uncleanness had to be dealt with actively, not passively" (Brooks, cited at Precept Austin).
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

**v. 13 — "Anyone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself defiles the tabernacle of the LORD. That person must be cut off from Israel."**

- Neglect was presumptuous sin. The defilement was not merely personal — it contaminated the sanctuary itself ("defiles the tabernacle of the LORD"). The penalty "cut off" (*karet*) is understood by many as death at the hand of God or excommunication from the covenant community (Gill, Guzik).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

---

## vv. 14–16 — Specific Cases of Defilement

**v. 14 — "Everyone who enters the tent and everyone already in the tent will be unclean for seven days."**

- Defilement from a corpse in an enclosed space was automatic and extended to everyone under that roof — whether they touched the body or not.

**v. 15 — "Any open container without a lid fastened on it is unclean."**

- An open vessel in the tent of the dead absorbed defilement. Constable notes the practical public-health dimension: these laws served to destroy potentially contaminated items, reducing disease spread. God's laws often carried both ceremonial/spiritual and practical/hygienic benefits.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html

**v. 16 — "Anyone in the open field who touches…a human bone or a grave, will be unclean for seven days."**

- The scope is comprehensive: death by violence ("slain by the sword"), natural causes, even touching a bone or grave. This made walking the wilderness — littered with graves after 38 years of dying — a constant risk of defilement. This shows God's mercy in providing the ash-water: without it, the nation would have been perpetually exiled from worship.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

---

## vv. 17–19 — The Application of the Cleansing Water

**v. 17 — "Take some of the ashes of the burnt sin offering, put them in a jar, and pour fresh water over them."**

- **"Fresh water"** — literally "living water" (*mayim chayyim*), i.e., water from a flowing spring or stream, not stagnant (Dummelow). Watson notes: "Special care was to be exercised that only living water, or water from a flowing stream, should be used for this purpose" (cited in Guzik).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/numbers-19.html

- The ashes and water together picture Christ's merit and the Spirit's work: "Signifying the ashes of Christ's merit, and the water of his Spirit" (Trapp, cited in Guzik). The water alone could not cleanse; the ashes alone would remain inert. Both must be combined.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

**v. 18 — "Then a man who is ceremonially clean is to take some hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle the tent, all the furnishings, and the people…"**

- A clean person (not a priest) performs the sprinkling — the rite was democratised, available in any Israelite settlement. The hyssop bunch served as the applicator, just as in the Passover (Ex 12:22) and the cleansing of the leper (Lev 14:4-6).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/19.htm

**v. 19 — "The man who is ceremonially clean is to sprinkle the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day. After he purifies the unclean person on the seventh day, the one being cleansed must wash his clothes and bathe in water, and that evening he will be clean."**

- Ellicott clarifies the pronouns: the rendering should be "he (the clean person) shall purify him (the unclean person), and he (the unclean person) shall wash his clothes…" The clean man is the agent; the unclean man also participates by washing himself.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-19.html

- The cleansing becomes effective at evening — a new day beginning, the person restored to the community of worship.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

---

## vv. 20–22 — Warnings and the Contagion of Uncleanness

**v. 20 — "But if a person who is unclean does not purify himself, he will be cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD."**

- Willful neglect equals contempt for God's provision. Guzik: "Uncleanness cannot correct itself. The unclean man will not just become clean over time. He must do something, and he must do what God says must be done to be clean."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

**v. 21 — "This is a permanent statute for the people: The one who sprinkles the water of purification must wash his clothes, and whoever touches the water of purification will be unclean until evening."**

- Even the "clean" man who applies the water becomes unclean until evening. And anyone merely *touching* the water (without a proper purpose) becomes unclean. This reinforces the paradox: what purifies the defiled defiles the pure who handle it casually. Guzik: "The one who regards the water of cleansing as a common thing will himself be regarded as unclean."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

**v. 22 — "Anything the unclean person touches will become unclean, and anyone who touches it will be unclean until evening."**

- **Contagion principle:** Uncleanness is easily transmitted (like a communicable disease), but cleanness must be deliberately obtained. This asymmetry teaches that holiness does not spread by casual contact — sin and death do.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

---

## The New Testament Connection: Hebrews 9:13-14

All commentators unite on the NT interpretation. The writer to the Hebrews explicitly uses the red heifer to show the superiority of Christ's sacrifice:

> "For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling the unclean, sanctifies for the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without spot to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" (Heb 9:13-14)

- The red heifer cleansed *flesh* (external, ceremonial); Christ's blood cleanses *conscience* (internal, moral).
- The heifer was without blemish → Christ was without spot (1 Pet 1:19).
- The heifer was slain outside the camp → Christ suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:11-12).
- The heifer's ashes were a permanent, ever-ready remedy → Christ's once-for-all sacrifice is perpetually effective.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/numbers-19.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ and Overlap

### Broad Agreement
All surveyed traditions (Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal, Methodist, Lutheran, Anglican) read Numbers 19 Christologically via Hebrews 9:13-14. The red heifer prefigures Christ. Differences are in emphasis and application, not in core exegesis.

### Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed Baptist)
Spurgeon preached a full sermon on the red heifer (1863, Metropolitan Tabernacle). His unique emphasis: the red heifer is specifically a picture of **Christ as the daily purification for believers' ongoing sins** — not initial justification, but continual cleansing for those already in covenant. He stresses: "From all the sins I ever shall commit there is a purification laid by to cleanse me." The heifer was female, he suggests, because it represents the whole Church (the Bride). The ashes laid by in a clean place picture Christ's enduring merits, always available. The water must be "running" (living) water — picturing the Holy Spirit's ever-fresh application of Christ's work.

- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-red-heifer
- https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons09.xli.html

### David Guzik / Enduring Word (Charismatic/Evangelical)
Guzik emphasises the *uniqueness* of this sacrifice at length — the colour, the female animal, the burning of blood with the carcass, the location outside the camp. His application is broadly evangelical: Christ's work is the better sacrifice that replaces the Levitical system. He also addresses modern interest in finding a red heifer for a third temple, cautioning that "in the Bible, there is nothing necessary about the water of purification made by the ashes of the burning of the red heifer. What it accomplished had already been made possible by a longer and more costly routine described in Leviticus 14."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

### Constable / Dallas Theological Seminary (Dispensational Evangelical)
Constable focuses on the historical context (mass deaths after Korah's rebellion) and the public-health dimensions. He notes the seven-day quarantine period aligns with incubation periods for most acute bacterial diseases, suggesting God's care for physical welfare alongside ceremonial teaching. He also references Jacob Milgrom's view that the rite was understood as exorcising a demon associated with corpse contamination (a view Constable reports but does not necessarily endorse).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html

### Pulpit Commentary / Homiletics (Broad Anglican/Protestant)
The Pulpit Commentary emphasises the didactic purpose of the paradox — that the clean become unclean while cleansing the unclean — as God's way of teaching the exceeding sinfulness of sin. It also draws a baptismal analogy: "At the door of the sanctuary there is still a laver. In the sacrament of baptism Christ says to every candidate for admission into his house, 'If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.'"

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/19.htm

## Catholic and Orthodox Readings

### Haydock Catholic Commentary
Haydock (19th century) reads the red heifer as a type of Christ's humanity — red, like the earth from which Adam was formed; without blemish, signifying Christ's sinlessness; never yoked, signifying freedom from sin. The burning outside the camp prefigures Christ's crucifixion outside Jerusalem. Haydock notes the Septuagint's translation "distinction" (*diastole*), which Augustine commented on (q. 33), seeing the rite as teaching the distinction between clean and unclean, holy and profane.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/19.htm

### Broader Catholic Interpretation
The water of purification with ashes is understood typologically as prefiguring the sacramental economy — especially baptism and penance — where physical elements (water, ashes) convey spiritual cleansing. The "permanent statute" points to the perpetual availability of cleansing in the Church. Catholic exegesis typically follows the patristic consensus that the red heifer is a type of Christ's sacrifice applied in the sacraments.

## Modern Scholarship

### Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges
Notes that the principle that contact with the dead causes pollution is "primitive and wide-spread," giving examples from America, Africa, Asia, Greece, and Rome. The chapter is an "isolated section of priestly writing" (P source), with vv. 1–13 and 14–22 possibly by different hands — the latter being "an expanded, and stricter, form." The use of the "water of impurity" was not universal in Israel; other purification methods for death-related defilement appear in Leviticus (5:2; 5:5-13; 11:24-28; 22:4-6).

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/19.htm

### NET Bible Notes (cited via Precept Austin)
The NET Bible note observes that Numbers 19 follows the section addressing priests and Levites (ch. 18) and now turns to the people. The red colour "suggested the blood of ritual purification," citing J. Milgrom, "The Paradox of the Red Cow (Num 19)," *Vetus Testamentum* 31 (1981): 62-72. Milgrom's thesis (cited also by Constable) is that the red heifer ritual was understood in its ancient context as an apotropaic rite to exorcise a demon of corpse contamination.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-19.html

## Modern Popular Teaching: End-Times Significance

Some modern evangelical and Pentecostal teachers see the search for a flawless red heifer in Israel as a sign of the end times. The Temple Institute announced a qualifying red heifer born in August 2018. According to Talmudic tradition, nine red heifers have been sacrificed in history; Maimonides taught the tenth would be offered by the Messiah Himself. Those anticipating a third temple believe red heifer ashes are essential for purifying the temple mount and priesthood. This view is most prominent in dispensational and some charismatic circles, though Guzik (a charismatic teacher) is cautious about overstating its necessity.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-19-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-19/

## Summary of the Traditional Christological Reading

All major traditions converge on this typology:

| Red Heifer | Christ |
|---|---|
| Female (bearer of life) | Source of resurrection life |
| Red | Covered in His own blood |
| Without blemish | Sinless (Heb 4:15; 1 Pet 1:19) |
| Never yoked | Never under sin's bondage |
| Slain outside the camp | Crucified outside Jerusalem (Heb 13:12) |
| Blood sprinkled 7× toward the sanctuary | Perfect, complete offering to God |
| Entirely burned, blood included | Total self-offering |
| Cedar, hyssop, scarlet added | Cross (wood), purification (hyssop), blood (scarlet) |
| Ashes stored for ongoing use | Once-for-all sacrifice, perpetually applied |
| Ashes + living water → cleansing | Christ's work + Holy Spirit → sanctification |
| Clean performers become unclean | Christ "made sin" for us (2 Cor 5:21) |
| Cleanses from death's defilement | Cleanses conscience from dead works (Heb 9:14) |
